title: Apostrophes, hyphens and quotation marks
note: Apostrophes mark possession and contractions, not ordinary plurals; possessive pronouns (its, hers, theirs) take none. Hyphenate a compound adjective before a noun ('a well-known author') but not after an -ly adverb. In American style, periods and commas go inside closing quotation marks; colons and semicolons go outside.

read.title: Small marks, big signals
text: The apostrophe has two jobs. It shows possession (the dog's bowl, the dogs' bowls) and it marks missing letters in a contraction (don't, it's). It almost never makes a plain plural. A sign reading "Fresh egg's" is wrong; the plural is eggs. The most famous trap is its versus it's. Its is a possessive pronoun, like his and hers, and possessive pronouns never take apostrophes. It's always means it is or it has.

Hyphens join words that work together as one adjective before a noun: a part-time job, a well-known author. After the noun the hyphen often drops: the job is part time. No hyphen follows an adverb ending in -ly, because the -ly already shows how the words connect: a carefully planned trip.

Quotation marks follow a firm American convention. Periods and commas go inside the closing mark: She called it "a disaster." Colons and semicolons go outside. Question marks and exclamation points go inside only when they belong to the quoted words.
